cards.title: let, const and inference
cards.body: `const` makes a binding you can't reassign; `let` makes one you can. You may annotate a type, as in `let limit: number = 3`, but usually tsc infers it from the starting value.
cards.tip: Default to `const`; reach for `let` only when the value must change.

code: let limit: number = 3;  // or annotate it

cards.title: One number type
cards.body: There is no separate int and float: every `number` is a 64-bit float, so `7 / 2` is `3.5` and `0.1 + 0.2` is not quite `0.3`. A failed conversion gives `NaN`, which isn't equal to anything, not even itself.
cards.tip: Test for it with `Number.isNaN(x)`, never `x === NaN`.

cards.title: Strings and template literals
cards.body: Strings take `'single'` or `"double"` quotes, and backtick strings fill in `${…}` with any expression. `+` with a string on either side joins text instead of adding.
cards.tip: `"1" + 2` is `"12"`, and tsc allows it: the result is a `string`.

cards.title: === vs ==
cards.body: `===` compares without converting types. `==` converts first, so in plain JavaScript `"7" == 7` is `true`. tsc rejects comparing a `string` with a `number` either way.
cards.tip: Always use `===` and `!==`. Convert on purpose with `Number(…)` or `String(…)`.

opts.label: id == 7
opts.error: error TS2367: This comparison appears to be unintentional because the types 'string' and 'number' have no overlap.
opts.note: Plain JavaScript would print `true` here. tsc stops you comparing unrelated types.

opts.label: id === "7"
opts.note: Same type on both sides, so `===` is a plain comparison.

opts.label: Number(id) === 7
opts.note: Convert explicitly, then compare two `number`s.

cards.title: null vs undefined
cards.body: JavaScript has two empty values: `undefined` means never set, and `null` means deliberately empty. With strict checks on, a `string` can hold neither; say so in the type, as in `string | null`.
cards.tip: `|` makes a union: `string | null` is a string or `null`.

opts.label: string
opts.error: error TS2322: Type 'null' is not assignable to type 'string'.
opts.note: Under strict checks, `null` is not a `string`.

opts.label: string | null
opts.note: The type allows `null`, so the assignment is fine.

opts.label: string | undefined
opts.note: `undefined` is a different value from `null`, with its own type.

cards.title: Truthy and falsy
cards.body: `if` accepts any value, not just a `boolean`. `false`, `0`, `""`, `NaN`, `null` and `undefined` count as false; everything else counts as true, even `"0"`.
cards.tip: To ask "is there a value?", compare with `null` instead: `score !== null`.

opts.note: Any number other than `0` and `NaN` is truthy.
`0` is falsy, so a real score of zero looks missing.

opts.label: null
opts.note: `null` is falsy, as intended.

name: Objects & arrays
blurb: Model data with object types, and predict aliasing

cards.title: Objects and object types
cards.body: An object literal groups named values: `{ name: "Ada", age: 36 }`. `type User = { … }` names a shape, and tsc checks that every `User` has each property with the right type.
cards.tip: A missing property is a type error: `{ name: "Ada" }` is not a `User`.

code: type User = { name: string; age: number };

cards.title: Shapes, not names
cards.body: tsc compares shapes, not type names: any object with a `name: string` fits `type Named = { name: string }`, even with extra properties. The exception is an object literal written straight into a typed slot, where an extra property is probably a typo.
cards.tip: This is called structural typing: a type is a list of what a value must have.

opts.label: user
opts.note: `user` has a `name: string`, so it fits `Named`. The extra `age` is fine.

opts.label: { name: "Ada", age: 36 }
opts.error: error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'age' does not exist in type 'Named'.
opts.note: A fresh literal typed as `Named` gets an excess-property check: nothing could ever read `age` through `n`.

opts.label: pet
opts.error: error TS2741: Property 'name' is missing in type '{ species: string; }' but required in type 'Named'.
opts.note: `pet` has no `name`, so its shape doesn't fit.

cards.title: Objects are references
cards.body: Assigning an object copies a reference, not the object: after `const b = a`, both names point at one object, so changing `b.x` changes `a.x`. `===` on objects asks "same object?", not "same contents?".
cards.tip: Two separate objects with equal contents are never `===`.

cards.title: const doesn't freeze
cards.body: `const` stops you rebinding a name, but you can still change the object it points to. To have tsc reject a property change, mark the property `readonly`, or add `as const` to make the whole literal read-only.
cards.tip: `readonly` and `as const` are checked by tsc only; they don't exist in the JavaScript that runs.

opts.label: just const
opts.note: `point` still names the same object; only its contents changed.

opts.label: readonly x
code: const point: { readonly x: number; y: number } = { x: 1, y: 2 };
opts.error: error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'x' because it is a read-only property.
opts.note: Only `x` is read-only here; `point.y = 5` would be fine.

opts.label: as const
code: const point = { x: 1, y: 2 } as const;
opts.error: error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'x' because it is a read-only property.
opts.note: `as const` makes every property of the literal `readonly`.

cards.title: Arrays
cards.body: `number[]` is an array of numbers. `map` makes a new array by transforming each element, and `filter` keeps the elements that pass a test; both take a function such as `(n) => n * 2`. Reading past the end gives `undefined`, yet tsc still types `words[5]` as `string`.
cards.tip: tsc can't see out-of-range reads, so that mistake only shows up when the code runs. Check the index against `words.length`.

demo.thrown: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toUpperCase')

cards.title: Spread copies one level
cards.body: `{ ...orig }` makes a new object with the same properties, and `const { name, tags } = orig` pulls properties out into variables. A spread copies only the top level: a nested array or object is still shared.
cards.tip: Copy a nested array too with `[...orig.tags]`.

opts.label: orig
opts.note: No copy at all: `copy` and `orig` are one object.

opts.label: { ...orig }
opts.note: `name` was copied, but `tags` is still the same array in both objects.

opts.label: { ...orig, tags: [...orig.tags] }
opts.note: The nested array is copied too, so `orig` is untouched.

name: Functions
blurb: Write typed functions and predict closures

cards.title: Parameter and return types
cards.body: Every parameter needs a type, as in `function area(w: number, h: number)`. A return type goes after the `)`, like `: number`; leave it off and tsc infers it from the `return`.
cards.tip: Unlike plain JavaScript, tsc checks every call: `area(3)` and `area("3", 4)` are both type errors.

code: function area(w: number, h: number): number {
function greet(name: string) {  // tsc infers string

cards.title: Arrow functions
cards.body: `(n: number) => n * 2` is a function written as a value: store it in a `const` and call it like any other function. Without braces, the expression after `=>` is returned; with braces, you need `return`.
cards.tip: With braces and no `return`, an arrow returns `undefined`, and tsc types its result as `void`.

code: const add = (a: number, b: number): number => {

cards.title: Optional and default parameters
cards.body: Passing too few arguments is a type error. `tip?: number` makes a parameter optional, so inside the function it's `number | undefined`; `tip = 0` makes it optional with a default, so it's always a `number`.
cards.tip: A left-out argument is `undefined`, and `10 + undefined` is `NaN`.

opts.label: tip: number
opts.error: error TS2554: Expected 2 arguments, but got 1.
opts.note: Both parameters are required, so tsc rejects `total(10)`. Plain JavaScript would run it with `tip` set to `undefined`.

opts.label: tip?: number
opts.note: The call is fine now, but `tip` is `number | undefined`, and tsc won't add `undefined` to a number.

opts.label: tip = 0
opts.note: A left-out `tip` becomes `0`, so it's always a `number`. tsc infers that type from the default.

cards.title: Functions are values
cards.body: You can store a function in a variable and pass it to another function, which calls it later: that's a callback. A function type such as `(n: number) => boolean` names the parameter types and the return type.
cards.tip: When tsc knows the expected function type, it infers the callback's parameter types, so `(n) => n > 10` needs no annotation.

code: function countIf(nums: number[], check: Check): number {

cards.title: Closures capture variables
cards.body: A function can use variables from the code around it, even after that code has finished running: it's called a closure. It captures the variable itself, not a copy of its value, so it sees whatever the variable holds when it's called.
cards.tip: Avoid `var`: it ignores `{ }` blocks, so every pass of a loop shares one variable.

opts.label: for (let i …)
opts.note: `let` in a `for` header makes a fresh `i` for each pass, so each function captures its own.

opts.label: for (var i …)
opts.note: `var` makes one `i` for the whole loop. The functions run after the loop, when that `i` is `3`.

opts.label: let i before the loop
opts.note: One `let i` shared by every pass behaves just like `var`: each function reads `i` when it's called, not when it was made.
